extracted.intended_audience: educated general public and engineers interested in thermodynamics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and physical principles for assessing the maximum possible efficiency of heat engines, based on the Carnot cycle, reversible engines, the absolute temperature scale, and practical constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversible engine as theoretical efficiency upper bound
rubrics_metrics.description: No heat-engine whatever can be more efficient than a reversible engine working between the same source and refrigerator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: if any engine A exceeded a reversible engine B, A could be used to run B backward and produce net work without net heat loss, constituting perpetual motion, which is impossible. Therefore the reversible engine yields the maximum mechanical effect for a given amount of heat taken from the source under the same temperatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a reversible heat-engine
rubrics_metrics.description: A reversible heat-engine is one which, running forward and performing a certain amount of work by means of a given amount of heat derived from a source, would, if run backward by the performance upon it of the same amount of work, restore to the source the same amount of heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although practically impossible, the conception is used theoretically: a reversible engine running backward restores all heat to the source and takes from the refrigerator the same heat it previously rejected. The reversible cycle is completely reversible in all physical and mechanical agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two physical axioms underpinning efficiency limits
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) Perpetual motion is impossible. 2) By inanimate material agency it is impossible to derive mechanical effect by cooling a portion of matter below the temperature of surrounding objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These axioms are used to eliminate impossible alternatives (e.g., deriving extra work by cooling below surroundings or constructing perpetual-motion schemes) and thus to justify that no engine can exceed the reversible engine's efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of efficiency among reversible engines
rubrics_metrics.description: All reversible engines working between the same source and refrigerator and taking the same amount of heat from the source must yield the same mechanical effect (i.e., have the same efficiency), regardless of working substance or construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, any convenient form of reversible engine may be assumed in theoretical discussions; results derived for one form (e.g., Carnot's with air) apply to all reversible engines operating between the same temperatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carnot cycle (four operations) as the reversible cycle model
rubrics_metrics.description: A reversible cycle consists of four operations (adiabatic compression, isothermal expansion at source temperature taking heat H, adiabatic expansion, and isothermal compression at refrigerator temperature giving heat h), and the work per cycle equals the area enclosed by the cycle on the p–V diagram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work done by the engine in one cycle is proportional to area B C D A (indicator diagram). Heat taken from the source is H, heat rejected to the refrigerator is h, and mechanical effect produced is H−h, so efficiency = (H−h)/H. The text gives detailed geometric/isothermal/adiabatic construction and area interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute temperature scale and proportionality of heats
rubrics_metrics.description: If T and t are temperatures on the absolute scale for the source and refrigerator of a reversible engine, then T:t :: H:h (heat received to heat rejected).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From this relation and the reversible-cycle properties one obtains the efficiency formula in temperature form. The text shows how an absolute scale may be constructed (using boiling and melting points of water as reference) and gives numerical conversions (e.g., boiling water ~671.4, melting ice ~491.4 on that scale when 180° separates them on Fahrenheit), leading to efficiency = 1 − t/T. Examples compute possible efficiencies for given temperature pairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency formula in terms of absolute temperatures
rubrics_metrics.description: The efficiency of a reversible engine working between absolute temperatures T (source) and t (refrigerator) is given by 1 − t/T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recapitulates that efficiency = (H−h)/H and, via the absolute temperature scale where H:h :: T:t, arrives at efficiency = 1 − t/T. Example: between boiling and freezing points of water the possible efficiency is about 27% (numerical example provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence of possible efficiency on temperature difference and practical limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportion of heat convertible into work increases as the refrigerator temperature is lower (or the temperature range between source and refrigerator is larger), but practical limits (ambient refrigerator temperature and difficulties achieving very high source temperatures) constrain achievable efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: with boiler pressure ~45 lb and vacuum of 25 in Hg (source ~294°F, refrigerator ~140°F), the theoretical maximum efficiency is ~20%, and actual engines give ~10–12% (over half the possible). Even with very high source temperatures (e.g., ~800°F) and modest refrigerator (~40°F), possible efficiency may be only ~60%. Concludes that large percentages of conversion are unlikely by practical means; improvements must increase temperature range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical alternative: direct conversion of chemical energy to electricity
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of converting chemical energy into heat and then into mechanical work, converting chemical energy directly into electric currents could permit much higher efficiency in producing mechanical effect or light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes existing electric machines convert 60–70% of electric energy into mechanical effect and that drives like a Brayton oil-engine coupled to a dynamo can be more efficient for lighting than burning in lamps. However, direct generation of electric currents from combustion presently requires high temperature and so still incurs energy waste; a discovery allowing direct and complete conversion would revolutionize power, light, and heating distribution.
